newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Students dance for democracy as Serbs demand change. [CORRECTED 22:14 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Students dance for democracy as Serbs demand change. [CORRECTED 22:14 GMT]

text.p: Down at the "Blue Cordon Disco" in the middle of a Belgrade street, students in a three-day standoff with police said on Tuesday they would dance for democracy until they got it.

"We will stay until the police move, because we want to have a beautiful country," 21-year-old Zivana said over the blare of American rock music from a sound system set up in the street, with a cordon of riot police just on the other side.

Thousands of students danced, talked to friends, read pamphlets and blew whistles on their side of the sound system, which blared Neil Young and AC/DC and was draped with a banner identifying the "Blue Cordon Disco".
The street on the other side of the speakers was guarded by the uniformed riot police and still belonged to the socialist government of President Slobodan Milosevic.

For more than two months Milosevic has resisted demands by the students, the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition and the international community to reinstate the results of November municipal elections in 14 cities won by Zajedno.

Students and Zajedno have held separate demonstrations, drawing crowds that at their peak reached half a million people, every day for more than two months, to force the government to accept the election results.

Most nights for the past month (corrects to clarify that students were allowed to march freely for the first month of protests) the police have blocked the students from marching. Then last week, after midnight, the police withdrew and the students marched around Belgrade.
On Sunday the policy changed again. The cordon stayed -- and so did the students.
"Who knows what the people in the government think?" said Nenad Vujovic, 23. "They probably want to make us tired and make us quit with the protest."
Vujovic, who has been demonstrating daily for 60 days and continuously since Sunday, said he had gone home to sleep for a few hours but would not give up.
"It is a long time, but we are fighting for something, for liberty," he said.
"I voted for a party (Zajedno) and I think that party can give us better results. Zajedno won but they (the government) doesn't care. They just say "We must win' and that's it."

Students, engineers, housewives, doctors, lawyers, teachers and even some of the blue-collar labourers deemed to be the hard-core Milosevic supporters spend their days and nights demonstrating against the government.

"I want change, a good situation for the country," said a man in his 50s who approached a reporter at a Zajedno rally in Belgrade. The man, who was afraid to give his name, said he had worked as a civil engineer around the world until jobs dried up when Yugoslavia was hit by sanctions during the Bosnia war.
"With Milosevic, we are deep below the earth," he said. "That is now where we are."

At a protest march earlier this week by thousands of people from some of the boroughs that make up Belgrade, retired English language teacher Dragana Albreht said Serbians wanted to show the world which slapped sanctions on them that they were ready and willing to change.
"We have had enough of everything. We have been separated from the world and we don't want that," Albreht said.
"I think that the students and the citizens want to become citizens of the world, not only of one small country.
"We have had enough of the politics of our leadership, we have had enough of poverty, we have had enough of war, we have had enough of nationalism.
"We have had enough of everything that separated us from the rest of the world."
